normalized.governing_thought: Fix gross margin and delivery economics rather than cutting labor: four quick moves protect the FY2026 covenant, and the full plan restores 3.0% by FY2028
executive_summary: The decline is mainly in gross margin and e-commerce, not wages. Operating margin fell 2.35 pts (3.37% → 1.02%). Gross margin lost 1.02 pts (promotions −0.70, shrink −0.50, private label +0.18) and e-commerce fulfillment 0.84 pts. Store labor cost only 0.30 pts, because 6% higher productivity absorbed most of the 9.4% wage rise.

Management's 8% labor cut would not reach the target. It saves $14.6M, but thinner staffing is linked to higher shrink worth an estimated $5–10M. FY2026 operating income would land at $19–24M against the $20M covenant, and FY2028 margin at only 0.9–1.2%.

A margin-led plan restores ~3.0% for ~$20M of one-time cost. Six levers backed by Harlow's own data (promotions, shrink, labor rebalancing, six lease lapses, private label, delivery fees) take operating income to ~$36M (2.5%) after the 2027 wage step. Three negotiated levers (vendor funding, three lease exits, the delivery contract) add ~$6M, for ~$42M, or 3.0%.

Act first on what is fast, cheap and proven, and hold contingencies. In the first 90 days: roll out the tested delivery fee, cancel money-losing promotions, protect fresh and receiving hours, and reject the 3% delivery-rate rise. FY2026 then reaches ~$24M (about $4M above the covenant). 3.0% has no cushion, so contingency levers are pre-agreed.
Decisions requested today: adopt this plan in place of the 8% labor cut; approve up to $20.5M of one-time spend; schedule a vote on exiting three long-lease stores.

slides.title: We started with a 'margin, not wages' hypothesis. The evidence supports the diagnosis, but commercial fixes alone reach only ~1.8%, so the answer had to grow

claims.claim: Initial hypothesis: the margin fell because of promotions, shrink and loss-making e-commerce growth, not wages, so Harlow can get back to 3% by fixing gross margin and e-commerce alone, with no labor action or store closures.
Labor is a minor cause of the decline — Supported
evidence: Labor explains 0.30 of the 2.35-pt fall (13%). Wage +9.4%, hours per $1,000 of sales −6%

claims.claim: Gross-margin erosion comes from drivers Harlow controls — Supported
evidence: Promo mix (−0.70), shrink (−0.50) and private label (+0.18) add up to the full −1.02 pts

claims.claim: The extra promotions are not paying back — Supported, but the response to ValuMart is uncertain
evidence: 38% of events lose money; vendor funding fell 55% → 46%; the 'more expensive' score rose 33% → 41%

claims.claim: E-commerce loses money and repricing fixes it — Partly: repricing helps but does not fix it
evidence: It loses ~$10.4M on an incremental basis. The fee test recovers ~$2.5M, but delivery still loses $9 per order

claims.claim: Gross-margin and e-commerce fixes alone reach 3% — Not supported
evidence: Promo, shrink, private label and fees add ~$18.8M, but the wage step and delivery rate (−$7.6M) leave ~$26.5M, or 1.8%

claims.claim: Revised answer: keep the gross-margin and e-commerce core, and add two levers the first hypothesis left out: (a) targeted labor productivity to absorb the 2027 wage step, rather than an 8% cut, and (b) exits from the weakest stores, starting with the six whose leases lapse by 2027. Vendor funding and the delivery contract close the last gap.

slides.title: Gross margin and e-commerce explain 80% of the 2.35-point fall in operating margin; store labor explains only 13%

claims.claim: Operating margin bridge FY2023 → FY2025
evidence: FY2023 margin 3.37%; Gross margin −1.02; E-commerce fulfillment −0.84; Store labor −0.30; Occupancy & energy −0.20; Other SG&A 0.00; FY2025 margin 1.02%

claims.claim: Gross margin (−1.02 pts, 43%): gross profit stayed flat while sales rose $83M
E-commerce (−0.84 pts, 36%): net fulfillment cost went from $5.2M to $18.1M as orders tripled
Labor (−0.30 pts, 13%): labor is the largest cost increase in dollars, which is why it looks like the cause, but most of that just tracked sales
Momentum: margin has fallen 1.10 and then 1.25 pts a year. One more year like FY2025 would take margin to about −0.2%, an operating loss, against a $20M covenant
Other SG&A was flat at 4.70% of sales

slides.title: Wages rose 9.4%, but 6% fewer hours per sales dollar absorbed most of it, so labor cost only 0.3 points of margin

claims.claim: Wage effect +1.11 pts; productivity effect −0.77 pts; net change in labor % of sales +0.34 pts
Wage inflation is real, but it is not the main cause; Harlow has already taken out about $12M through productivity
evidence: at FY2023 productivity, FY2025 labor would have cost $193.9M ($18.38 × 7.02 ÷ 1,000 × $1,503M) instead of $181.9M

claims.claim: Productivity gains have not been free: shrink rose and it is highest in the stores with the fewest hours
evidence: shrink rose from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales

claims.claim: Labor still needs action, because the 2027 minimum-wage step adds ~$7M; the plan offsets most of it through targeted scheduling rather than an across-the-board cut
Table 3 inputs are rounded, so the net (+0.34) differs slightly from Table 1 (+0.30)

slides.title: Promotions (−0.70 pts) and shrink (−0.50 pts) account for the whole 1.02-point gross-margin fall; private label offset only 0.18

claims.claim: Gross-margin change by driver
evidence: Promo share of sales 24.0% → 29.0%, +5.0 pts × −14 pts = −0.70

claims.claim: Promotions are the largest single driver: every extra point of promo share costs ~$2.1M a year
Shrink is the second: every 0.1 pt is ~$1.5M a year
The three drivers explain all of it, so there is no unexplained cost or price residual left to chase

slides.title: The promotion surge is not buying the traffic it was meant to defend: 38% of events lose money and price perception got worse

claims.claim: 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money, even after counting the extra units they sold
Harlow now pays more of each markdown itself
evidence: share of promotional markdowns funded by vendors 55% → 46%, FY2023 → FY2025

claims.claim: Price perception got worse despite five more points of promoted sales
evidence: customers who say Harlow is 'more expensive than other options' 33% → 41%

claims.claim: Deeper promotions did not protect stores near ValuMart
evidence: FY2025 comparable sales −4.2% within 3 miles of a new ValuMart vs +1.1% other stores

claims.claim: The category team's evidence does not hold up
evidence: The claim: stores with the deepest promotions grew comps 1.8% against 0.2% for the rest (+1.6 pts)
1.6% × 20% contribution = 0.32 pts of sales. That pays for only 2.3 pts of extra promo share (0.32 ÷ 0.14), and the chain added 5.0 pts
It is a correlation: it says nothing about the 38% of events that lose money, or about profit

claims.claim: Cut the losing events first; there is a clear profit case, and the risk sits mainly in ValuMart-exposed stores
Make vendor funding a condition of running an event, to restore part of the 9-pt funding drop
Compete on value through private label and fresh produce, not through deeper national-brand markdowns
evidence: fresh produce, the #1 reason to shop Harlow (58%)

§7 survey (70% would otherwise buy in store)

slides.title: We ask the board for three decisions today and propose five measures to track progress every quarter

claims.claim: Replace the draft plan: adopt the margin-led plan and a FY2028 target of at least 3.0% in place of the 8% labor-hour cut. Keep the freeze for home delivery only.
Approve the capital: up to $20.5M of one-time spend over FY2026–FY2028, with the remaining $4.5M held in reserve and released by the board.
Set up the store vote: bring the case for the three long-lease stores to the Q3 FY2026 meeting. Non-renewal of the six expiring leases is the default.
Quarterly KPIs (FY2025 → FY2028 target)

What changes for management: category team measured on promotion profit, not comps; e-commerce team reports contribution including delivery on an incremental basis; store operations measured on shrink as well as labor hours. These changes fix the three measurement errors that hid the decline.

alternatives_considered.option: A Management plan: 8% labor cut, freeze e-commerce
alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject. FY2026 $19–24M, at risk if shrink responds; FY2028 0.9–1.2%; acts on the 13% of the decline that came from labor and creates new shrink risk; does not address 87% of the decline.

alternatives_considered.option: B Defend on price: deeper promotions vs ValuMart
alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject. FY2026 below $15M (each +1 pt of promo share costs $2.1M); FY2028 under 1%; margin erosion with no evidence of traffic payback.
Adopt (recommended). FY2026 ~$24M with ~$4M headroom; FY2028 ~3.0%; ~$20M one-time; payback under one year; main risk is executing nine levers at once and ValuMart response.

alternatives_considered.option: D Plan C, then exit home delivery
alternatives_considered.treatment: Hold as a fallback. Up to ~3.5% (+$6M at most), but breaks an owner commitment (owners want delivery kept) and risks customer loss.

alternatives_considered.option: Initial hypothesis: fix gross margin and e-commerce alone, with no labor action or store closures
alternatives_considered.treatment: Not supported: leaves ~$26.5M, or 1.8%; answer revised to add labor productivity and store exits.

Rejected: the three long-lease stores have the weakest payback (3.4–4.1 years) and need a board vote; waiting two quarters costs ~$1.1M but avoids paying $7.5M to exit stores the fixes might turn around.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: All FY2028 figures are run-rate on the FY2025 sales base, with FY2025 prices and volumes; no like-for-like sales growth and no inflation other than the known 2027 wage step.
3.0% has no cushion: each key risk would cost about 0.2–0.3 points; combined downside gives 2.32% ($32M).
Response to ValuMart to fewer promotions is uncertain; 15% of shifted promo volume assumed lost (30% downside).
The time-series shrink–labor link is a correlation, used as a risk range, not a forecast; equal sales weight per quartile assumed.
Sales risk from longer checkout waits and stock-outs is untested; how customers react to the labor changes is untested.
30% of online sales are new to Harlow (survey); the fee test (4 stores, 10 weeks) is assumed to scale chain-wide; lost sales valued at 20% contribution.
Wage step +4% applied to the whole store labor bill (conservative).
The six and three stores are pro-rata shares of the nine-store totals; store-level data should confirm before each lease decision; closure costs ~$0.5M per store are a team assumption.
Only the $7.5M lease-exit cost comes from the pack; all other one-time amounts are team estimates to be confirmed by Finance.
The 14-pt promo margin gap is read as net of vendor funding (drives the ~$90M vendor-pool estimate).
Fiscal timing: FY2026 treated as the first plan year; if FY2026 has already closed by February 2027, the covenant test is settled and Year 1 shifts to FY2027.
Whether occupancy and SG&A keep rising faster than sales (+0.2 pt in FY2023–25).
FY2026 bridge assumes the FY2023–25 drift stops once the actions start.
All choices were made without access to management; each should be confirmed before the board meeting.
next_steps: Wave 1 (first 90 days): roll out $7.99 fee / $100 free-delivery threshold; cancel failing promotions with 'no funding, no feature'; stop the 8% cut and ring-fence fresh and receiving hours; reject the 3% delivery rate rise and tender the contract.

Wave 2 (FY2026 H2 – FY2027): do not renew the six expiring leases; demand-based scheduling in Q3–Q4 stores (−3% hours); fresh-waste and receiving program; private-label range expansion and vendor-funding round.
